A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Forking-Sequences. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, moved, revised, and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting comparisons on 16 competition datasets, convergence experiments, a covariance simulation, and ensembling analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original revised forecasting experiments and additional synthetic gradient, foundation-model ensembling, and quantile-coverage results.

M1.justification: Shared encoding, all-FCD training losses, and the quantile objective remain. v2 extends the inference ensemble options with exponential smoothing that weights recent forecasts more heavily, recommending alpha=0.9, beyond v1’s moving mean, median, and cumulative averaging.

E1.justification: The 16 competition subsets remain, but v2 adds synthetic-data pretraining with cross-frequency and zero-shot foundation-model evaluation, plus synthetic oscillatory data for gradient analysis. Its linear convergence study replaces M1 Monthly data with synthetic AR(1) processes at four autocorrelation levels.

E2.justification: v2 adds S4 to the corresponding FS-versus-WS benchmark comparisons and evaluates NBEATS and PatchTST ensembles against their unensembled versions in Figures 8 and 16. The original five MQForecaster encoder types and ETS/ARIMA comparators remain.

E3.justification: v1’s largely fixed 30,000-step configurations become five-trial Optuna searches with 45,000 steps and revised parameter ranges. v2 separates unensembled benchmark results from ensemble effects, introduces sEV evaluation, and emphasizes median cross-dataset improvements. The original temporal splits remain; new gradient and coverage experiments introduce additional testing procedures.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct LSTM/Transformer gradient-flow analysis and quantile-coverage sensitivity tests. It replaces the original window-count/learning-rate convergence ablation with an autocorrelation-controlled GD-versus-SGD study and substantially expands quantitative ensemble comparisons, including smoothing strengths and foundation models.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations over five runs. v2 additionally specifies 20 repetitions and gradient signal-to-noise estimation in Appendix B.1; the replacement linear experiment records seed 42 instead of v1’s seed 1.

E6.justification: The benchmark results are extensively replaced under revised settings. For example, M1 Monthly RNN FS/WS sCRPS changes from 0.1283/0.1678 in v1 Table 1 to 0.654/0.890 in v2 Table 2, not a same-setting performance comparison. v2 also adds S4, sEV, gradient, foundation-model, and coverage outcomes.

T1.justification: v2 retains the gradient-variance theorem but removes v1’s formal forecast-ensemble convergence theorem. It adds gradient-flow propositions, encoder-specific complexity proofs, and the EV definition and property theorem. Restricted-attention complexity changes from O(T²L) to O(TL²). The new EV penalty identities are inconsistent with their case analysis in Table 5.

C1.justification: v2 makes EV and mitigation of vanishing gradients central contributions and extends accuracy-preserving stability claims to foundation models. The abstract shifts from average sQPC reductions to median accuracy gains and separately measured ensemble stability improvements. sQPC itself was already introduced in v1.

C2.justification: v2 expands the existing accuracy–stability discussion with uncertainty in older forecasts, recency-weighting explanations, and inconclusive calibration effects. It adds univariate, memory, and heterogeneous-series limitations, while replacing v1’s minimal-tuning caveat. It also distinguishes useful forecast revisions from harmful volatility.

D1.justification: Appendix G documents Optuna selection criteria and encoder-specific search spaces in place of fixed configurations. New appendices specify synthetic generators, gradient-study architectures, and simulation parameters. v2 also identifies NeuralForecast defaults for its foundation-model implementations, although their synthetic pretraining data remain sparsely described.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating related work, v2 adds substantive comparisons with stability-specific losses and postprocessing, including Belle et al. and Caljon et al. It develops the distinction between target replication and teacher forcing and adds positioning around quantile aggregation, state-space models, and cross-frequency forecasting.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work and the temporal-split description move into the main text, contributions are reorganized, and appendices are substantially restructured. Terminology shifts toward architectural design, alongside author and affiliation changes.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the architecture diagram to show the forecast grid, corrects date axes, and marks forecast revisions. It adds gradient and coverage plots, expands ensemble displays into large multipanel figures, and restructures complexity, hyperparameter, and result tables. Several retained figures also move between the main text and appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens v1’s minimally tuned validation with tuning, gradient tests, foundation-model experiments, and explicit ensemble/calibration tradeoffs. However, the new EV theorem contradicts its definition and Table 5: at q=0.5, its stated nonzero penalties are half those obtained from the definition. Appendix J also repeats v1’s positive sQPC summaries despite Table 15 showing worse RNN/LSTM stability, and leaves a percentage unfilled. These defects affect central theory and result interpretation, making the net quality improvement uncertain.
